title: The Houses of Unequal Stars
summary: An intentional community mistakes a useful star classification for social destiny while a provisional boundary becomes an inherited border.
history: In 914, island reformers built a community where work rotated according to declared inclination rather than inherited household status. An observer arranged stars by color and apparent brightness, discovering that similar lights could stand at very different distances. Enthusiasts assigned household tasks according to the star table, converting a warning against superficial resemblance into a system of fixed personal destiny. Mainland patrons supplied scribes and introduced a prestigious administrative language distinct from everyday speech. A peace conference divided the islands temporarily between rival custodians. The promised review never occurred, and the community’s experiments became competing traditions on opposite sides of a supposedly provisional line.
question: whether a common work calendar can cross the old partition without restoring either the star castes or the patrons’ exclusive scribal authority.
transformations: Intentional communities and a reorganization of work around human inclination inspire a cooperative settlement with contested practical results.
Classification by color and brightness, together with errors in distance estimation, becomes naked-eye comparative astronomy without importing modern instruments.
A composite elite culture and continuity of an administrative language become patronage shared across several island populations.
A ceasefire’s provisional partition and unrealized political review become an island boundary whose temporary character has been forgotten.
rows: Fen of the Rotating Tables

Fen proposed changing unpopular tasks every seventh day, then exempted skilled scribes from rotation. Workers challenged the exception without rejecting the community. Her revised notes admit that inclination can conceal convenience when people differ in bargaining power.
The Star Court Orchard

Night observers used orchard walls to block lamp glare. Later priests grafted trees according to alleged stellar temperaments, ruining several varieties. Gardeners restored compatible rootstocks while keeping the observation benches, preserving useful inquiry without its failed agricultural doctrine.
The Houses of Inclination

Households advertised chosen work and exchanged labor through a public table. Rich members could choose pleasant tasks more readily. A disputed account records who cleaned after festivals, showing the hidden work beneath declarations that everyone followed a beloved calling.
The Provisional Island Division

Negotiators divided landing custody for one fishing season and promised a review after storm damage was assessed. The review funds financed a memorial instead. Descendants treat the division as ancient, although the founding document repeatedly describes its term as temporary.
The Two Brightness Boards

One board lists apparent brightness; the other compares recurring changes over years. Patrons displayed only the first, making distant lights seem equivalent to near ones. The second survives in a net loft whose owner wants recognition for keeping it dry.
The Unchosen Task Meal

Participants serve a meal made through tasks they would not personally choose, acknowledging dependence beyond inclination. Affluent members hire replacements. Organizers now require disclosure of paid assistance rather than claiming that private labor can be made equal by ceremony.
The Color Without Rank

An observer’s manuscript states that a star’s color supplies no household rank. Later margin notes turn the classification into a destiny chart. Readers reproduce the layers separately, allowing believers to see which authority their preferred system actually invokes.
The Lantern Reef Ray

A translucent ray follows small fish attracted by quay lamps. Star-house interpreters describe its visits as celestial confirmation. Fishers reduce lamps near its breeding shallows, demonstrating that controlling the apparent sign protects the animal without settling anybody’s cosmic beliefs.
The Review Ferry

The ferry once transported delegates to the promised boundary review. Its seasonal landing rights remain valid despite the abandoned conference. Current passengers invoke those finite rights to cross between islands whose patrols now claim no lawful connection ever existed.
The Seasonal Partition Term

This clause expires custodial division after one season unless all named landing households renew it. Officials cite later decrees instead of renewal evidence. The law’s recovery threatens patrol income more directly than either island’s identity.
Aser of the Distant Lamp

Aser showed that two equally bright shoreline lamps could differ in distance and size. His demonstration used ordinary oil and measured ropes. Followers embellished it into an ability to command stars, obscuring the patient comparisons he wanted neighbors to repeat.
The Shared Script Hall

The hall taught a patron’s formal language while everyday accounts remained in several local tongues. Students learned to translate obligations rather than erase differences. Later custodians banned vernacular margins, weakening the very accuracy that justified the school’s prestige.
The Unranked Observers

Observers recruit gardeners, navigators, and roof repairers to compare conditions affecting the sky. Elite patrons want membership restricted to polished readers. The group’s response is a public record identifying each practical contribution, making exclusion costly to its own evidence.
The Orchard Temperament Failure

Star-based grafting killed trees unevenly because rootstocks differed. Leaders blamed gardeners’ impure inclination. A surviving planting map correlates losses with graft compatibility, exposing how a flattering cosmic explanation concealed a testable practical mistake.
The Rotation Tokens

Tokens assign unpleasant communal tasks and record substitutes. One series lacks substitute marks, making affluent households appear exemplary. Restoring the omitted marks changes who owes labor without requiring a claim that every founder acted dishonestly.
The Two Language Supper

Hosts recite each undertaking in the patron’s language and a household’s chosen tongue. Mistakes are corrected before food is served. Younger speakers propose a third version for migrants, extending a custom whose original defenders once treated two languages as sufficient forever.
The Conference Afterword

A clerk preserved delegates’ disagreements beneath the formal boundary agreement. The afterword reveals doubts about maintenance funding rather than a secret wish for permanent division. Its recovery makes the missing review a failure of execution as well as political will.
The Stars in the Cistern

One courtyard cistern reflects stars displaced by irregular stonework around its lip. Islanders call the pattern a second sky. Observers use it to demonstrate how a meaningful image can arise from local geometry and still carry a household’s cherished history.
Night Oil Sharing

Observers pool lamp oil but shade every light during comparisons. Their finite supply limits meetings in winter. Patrons offer endless symbolic devotion and little oil, prompting a plain subscription ledger that values practical contributions over ceremonial pledges.
The Border’s Missing Review

Landing workers demand the original review because their work calendars cross the partition. Rival custodians accuse them of abolishing tradition. The workers seek inspection of actual costs first, leaving political arrangements negotiable rather than prejudged by either accusation.
